summary: A 1975 working document specifying a front-end protocol for attaching a Burroughs B6700 computer to an ARPA-style network. The approach is to use a front-end processor with a new protocol, built on earlier concepts from RFC 647.

plainLanguage.summary: A big computer was too busy to talk to the network itself. This note describes a helper machine that does the talking for it.

questions: what is a front end processor
how does fep abstract network complexity
subtitle: A protocol for letting a helper processor manage network access.

tldr.problem: A large mainframe computer like the Burroughs B6700 is too busy to implement the full complexity of ARPANET protocols. But it needs network access.
tldr.mechanism: The Front-End Protocol (FEP) lets a smaller processor (the front-end) handle all ARPANET protocol details. The host and FE communicate through simple commands (BEGIN, LISTEN, MESSAGE, END) that abstract away socket management, protocol translation, and connection state.
tldr.outcome: The B6700 gains network access with minimal intrusion into its operating system. The front-end handles RFC negotiation, socket assignment, and data translation. The host sees only high-level conversation paths.

facts.value: 7 (BEGIN, LISTEN, MESSAGE, INTERRUPT, END, REPLY, RESPONSE)

today: RFC 705 is a working document for a specific front-end protocol for the B6700. The front-end delegation model remains relevant: modern systems often use proxy servers and load balancers to abstract network complexity from application servers, following the same architectural principle.

sections.title: The Front-End Approach
sections.content:
The ARPANET requires every host to implement a complex Network Control Program (NCP) that handles protocols, socket management, error recovery, and data formatting. This is a substantial engineering burden. An alternative is to use a front-end processor: a smaller, simpler computer that attaches directly to the network and relays data to the main host. The main host does not see network complexity; it just tells the FE what to do.

RFC 705 is a working document describing such a protocol for the Burroughs B6700, a large mainframe. The protocol is built on earlier work by Padlipsky and others (RFC 647) and has been implemented and tested at NSA and ACC.
sections.plainLanguage: When a big powerful computer needs the network, it can hire a small helper machine to handle the boring protocol details.

sections.title: Commands and Paths
sections.content:
Communication between the host and front-end is entirely command-based. The main commands are:

  • BEGIN: The host directs the FE to establish one or more network connections to a foreign host, specifying the target address and socket.
  • LISTEN: The host tells the FE to wait for incoming connection requests from the network.
  • MESSAGE: Data is sent in MESSAGE commands. The FE forwards host messages to the network and delivers network data back to the host.
  • END: Close one or more connections.
  • INTERRUPT: Signal an urgent condition, such as a user pressing Control-C.
  • REPLY: Acknowledge receipt and report success or failure of a command.

Each conversation is identified by an INDEX (assigned by the host). Within an index, data flows on one or more PATHS. A path can be SEND (host to network only), RECEIVE (network to host only), or DUPLEX (bidirectional). The FE assigns actual network sockets transparently.
sections.plainLanguage: The host gives commands like "connect to this computer", "listen for calls", "send this data". The helper FE handles all the network details and tells the host when it is done.

sections.title: Socket and Protocol Abstraction
sections.content:
The ARPANET Host-Host Protocol defines connections between sockets (each socket is identified by a host number and a 32-bit socket number). The FE shields the host from managing sockets directly. When a host issues a BEGIN command to establish a new conversation, the FE selects appropriate sockets based on the connection type. For well-known services, the host can use the Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) mode, where the host specifies a well-advertised socket and the FE negotiates an actual working socket with the remote host.

The FE also handles data translation: the host can specify different data formats for the network (e.g., ASCII, EBCDIC) and the FE performs the translation automatically.

Flow control is managed by REPLY commands. The sender is blocked until a REPLY is received, ensuring ordered delivery and allowing the receiver to signal when it is ready for more data.
sections.plainLanguage: The host does not have to think about socket numbers or how to talk to the network. It just says what it wants, and the FE figures out the details.

sections.title: Benefits for the Host
sections.content:
By delegating to a front-end, the B6700 avoids a large and complex NCP implementation. The host's operating system is minimally disrupted. The host can express networking in terms of high-level conversations rather than low-level protocol state. The FE handles timeouts, retransmissions, connection state, and all the machinery that ARPANET operations require.

This approach allows large, busy systems to participate in the ARPANET without the substantial software engineering investment of a full NCP implementation on the host itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The big computer stays focused on what it does best, while the helper handles the network boring stuff.
